messages.content: No two consecutive words can share the same first letter. In the USA, if a copyright infringement case has been decided by the judicial system to be fair use, is it more accurate to say that a) copyright infringement occurred but it was legally excused, or b) copyright infringement did not occur?

message.content: Option b is more accurate. When courts determine fair use, the use does not constitute infringement. Fair use is a recognized defense that negates the claim of copyright infringement. The use was never infringing to begin with.

The legal answer: Fair use is an affirmative defense to copyright infringement. When a court finds fair use, the typical legal framing is that the use was "fair" — meaning it does not constitute infringement. The Supreme Court in Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music (1994) described fair use as "an equitable rule of reason." The prevailing view is that fair use means the use was NOT an infringement — it's not that infringement occurred and was excused. Fair use is a defense that negates the claim of infringement. So option (b) is more accurate: copyright infringement did not occur.
